3. In their previous work (Bailles et al., 2019 Nature, ref#6), it was stated that MyoII wave dynamics
is independent of Fog delivery based on the result that a higher Fog copy number did not increase
the speed of wave propagation. This conclusion appears to contradict the current work. I understand
that these conclusions are based on different experiments, and no data is contradictory. However,
including the results section below requires a more thorough explanation of why the authors propose
opposite interpretations.
“Although previous studies (reference cited for #6) ruled out that the propagation of MyoII activation
reflects the propagation of a wavefront of diffusion/transport of the ligand Fog, the role of Fog-
GPCR signalling in activating MyoII in cells of the PZ was not directly tested. Furthermore, the
absence of integrins (KO of the 𝛼-PS3 integrin, Scab) does not completely abolish MyoII activation,
which remains pulsatile at low levels, during wave propagation, indicating that other factors, such
as Fog-GPCR signalling, could be involved.”
Response: The reviewer raises a valid point and we agree that we need to better clarify the apparent
contradiction between the conclusions in our previous study and those in this study.
In a nutshell in Bailles and Collinet et al., 2019 we showed that Fog diffusion/delivery does not
determine the dynamics of the MyoII wave, such as if the wave reflected the non-steady state
dynamics of a diffusion front. We add now that Fog delivery is nonetheless required to make a
gradient to begin with. The wave reflects the propagation of a steady state gradient pattern.
In our previous study (Bailles and Collinet et al., 2019 Nature, PMID: 31413363) we falsified the
hypothesis that the propagation of MyoII activation reflected the dynamic expansion of a Fog gradient
before reaching a steady state, due to diffusion and degradation. In this case the expansion speed of
the gradient would decay over time as would the amplitude at the front. To account for the observed
wave kinematics (constant speed of propagation and constant amplitude) we considered a model that
couples Fog diffusion and saturable receptor binding and compared its predictions with experiments.
While the model predicts that increasing Fog production at the source should increase the speed of
the MyoII wave propagation, the experiments showed that this remained constant despite increased
MyoII levels in cells of the PZ. We also showed that the homogenous overexpression of fog in the
5
entire embryo did not abolish the wave propagation of MyoII in the PZ and we concluded that the
wave dynamics of MyoII activation, i.e. its propagation in the PZ, does not solely depend on a
wavefront of Fog protein delivery (we wrote “patterned Fog signalling does not determine the
dynamics of the MyoII wave. Fog may be required, but MyoII activation is not governed solely by
Fog-dependent Rho1 activation in the propagation region.”). Notably, this conclusion leaves the door
open and even suggests that Fog signalling may be required, but together with other factors (e.g.
contact with the vitelline membrane, activation of integrins and their modulation of signalling from
GPCR).
Here we propose that Fog needs to diffuse to form an activity gradient that is at a steady state at any
moment in front of the invaginating furrow. The wave reflects and is coupled to the movement of the
self-organized reconstitution of the gradient (which involves tissue contact with the VM, integrin
activation, receptor clustering, etc.). If tissue movements were blocked, the gradient would maintain
its shape and position.
We now better explain this at the beginning of the result section (pp.3, lines 23-25) and we inserted a
paragraph in the discussion (pp. 10, lines 35-41).
We write at the beginning of the result section: “Previous studies6 ruled out that the propagation wave
of MyoII activation solely reflects the anterior movement of the diffusion front of an expanding
gradient of the ligand Fog away from the endoderm primordium.”
and in the discussion: “Notably, this is not inconsistent with previous reports excluding the possibility
that the wave propagation of MyoII recruitment towards the anterior solely reflects the expansion of
a non-steady state gradient of the ligand Fog diffusing away from the endoderm primordium6. If this
were the case the expansion rate of the gradient would decay over time. Instead, the speed of
propagation and the amplitude of the MyoII gradient in front of the invaginating furrow are constant.
Therefore, the wave of MyoII recruitment reflects a steady-state activity gradient of the ligand Fog
that is constantly renewed as it travels anteriorly across the tissue.”.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript “Spatial patterning of contractility by a mechanogen gradient underlies Drosophila
gastrulation” by Mundhe et al., presents evidence of the existence of mechanogens, molecular
gradients that spatially control cell mechanics in a concentration dependent manner. Using the
Drosophila gastrulating embryo, the authors show that the GPCR ligand Fog is expressed in the
posterior endoderm and diffuses towards the propagation zone (PZ) of an actomyosin contractility
wave. Using live imaging, FCS and genetic perturbations they show that although Fog is distributed
uniformly in the extracellular space, it forms a surface-bound gradient. The authors propose that this
gradient generates patterns of receptor oligomerization and endocytosis resulting in Myosin-II
activity gradient. Last, the interplay of Fog/actomyosin and vitelline membrane attachment via
integrins is further investigated leading to the conclusion that integrins self-renew this gradient.
Overall, the experiments are rigorous and the quantitative analysis is accurate. The existence of a
mechanogen, which is the main goal of this paper, is very convincing, changing our view of how
diffusive molecules can drive patterning, beyond eliciting transcription-dependent responses. Below
some comments that (in my opinion) can prove even further the existence of a pure “mechanogen”
and clarify the proposed mechanistic interplay between Fog/Smog/Myosin and integrins.
Major comments:
6
• Transcription-dependency. According to the definition of a “mechanogen” given by the authors,
such a diffusive molecule should trigger changes in cell mechanics directly, meaning that an
intermediate step involving transcription is not required. Can the authors support somehow the claim
that indeed transcription is dispensable for Fog-dependent Myosin-II gradient?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. In a previous study (Bailles and Collinet et
al., 2019 Nature, PMID: 31413363) we provided evidence that the propagation of MyoII activation
is independent of gene transcription. We reported that the injection of α-amanitin, a potent inhibitor
of the RNA polymerase, did not block the wave propagation of MyoII activation, which occurred
with kinetics similar to WT embryos (Fig. 2 in that paper). We now provide new data where we
directly analyzed the effects of blocking gene transcription on the formation and maintenance of the
gradient of MyoII that we describe here. Our results show that in embryos injected with α-amanitin
MyoII forms a gradient similar to WT embryos and that the gradient remains unchanged over time.
We conclude that the establishment of the MyoII gradient does not require gene transcription. These
data are shown in a new Fig. S4B-D.
• Length-scales of Myosin vs Smog oligomerization vs Fog ligand. The steepness of the MyoII
gradient does not match the steepness neither of Fog (as the authors mention) nor of the oligomerized
receptor. The authors showed compelling evidence for Smog receptor oligomerization patterns being
responsible for the Fog-dependent GPCR activation, but still is the Smog oligomerization length-
scale as steep as the myosin length-scale? Another possibility is that the expression of Smog is pre-
patterned as a steep gradient, where cells closer to the myosin front express much more Smog than
cells further away. This would also fit with the observation that despite the high extracellular
abundance of Fog (84%), it is not contributing to longer-range signalling in the PZ. Could this be
this be due to the absence of Smog from cells further away and thus they cannot receive excess Fog?
Response: We answer these two great questions below:
Steepness of the MyoII and Smog oligomerization gradient: In front of the invaginating furrow
Smog brightness decreases by about half of its dynamic range, i.e. the max brightness (corresponding
approximately to that of trimers) minus the min brightness (corresponding approximately to that of
monomers), within a range of about 30 µm, similar to the Fog fraction. More precisely, the
slow
oligomer fraction decreases to half of its initial value (measured at distance 0) at a distance of 30-35
µm (e.g. from 26% to 13% trimers or 100% to 50% dimers). As noted by the reviewer, this decrease
is less steep compared to the decrease of MyoII intensity, which in the same region decreases more
than 10 folds and follows an exponential decay. This is not unexpected since the signalling cascade
that leads to MyoII activation downstream of GPCRs includes many steps (interactions with integrins,
activation of heterotrimeric G proteins, Rho1, Rock, etc.) which may lead to non-linear signal
amplification and thus increase the steepness of the MyoII gradient. In fact, we know that integrins
are part of this amplification (based on the shape of the gradient in the αPS3 mutant, Fig. 6B and
S7D, now S8D).
Is the MyoII gradient due to a gradient of Smog receptor?: The Smog receptor is expressed
homogenously in the epithelial blastoderm (Kerridge et al 2016, PMID: 26780298). Therefore, the
MyoII gradient does not depend on a gradient of total Smog receptor. Furthermore, a pre-patterned
gradient of expression of the receptor would provide a static protein gradient in the referential of the
tissue with high concentration close to the primordium and lower concentrations at a distance. If the
gradient of MyoII was due this static gradient of receptor, then its amplitude and the range would
decrease over time as the invagination front (and thus the MyoII gradient) moves across the tissue
and, therefore across gradient of receptor. This is not what we observe. We observe that the MyoII
7
gradient maintains a constant amplitude and range over time despite the movement of the invaginating
furrow across the tissue (Fig. 3C). Note that this is also true when de novo transcription is blocked,
which rules out that expression of a putative co-receptor propagates as a wave to shape the gradient.
The constant amplitude and range of the gradient is naturally emerging from the self-organized
mechanism that we propose here.
For a putative co-factor/co-receptor to be involved, its activation would have to be part of the
mechanism of gradient formation. The co-factor could be expressed in a fixed but broad enough
domain to encompass the whole PZ, and some specific event would potentiate its activity, for instance
the contact with the VM. This is precisely what we document for integrins. Once expressed in the PZ
before induction of wave propagation, integrin transcription is no longer required and integrin activity
is potentiated/activated by the contact to the VM which itself propagates as a wave.
Altogether, these data and these considerations support the fact that the MyoII gradient does not
simply emerge from a gradient of the Smog receptor expression/protein concentration and this is not
what limits longer-range signalling in the PZ.
We now discuss this more explicitly in the discussion (pp. 11, lines 22-35).
“The self-organized Fog activity gradient is constantly renewed over time. This feature allows the
gradient to maintain a constant amplitude and range over time as it translocates with the moving
front of tissue invagination towards the embryo anterior. In contrast, a gradient deterministically
controlled by a hierarchical mechanism (e.g. by the concentration gradient of a factor, e.g. a receptor
or a co-factor/co-receptor, at the beginning of the invagination process) would not display such a
feature and its amplitude and range would progressively decrease over time as the furrow moves
anteriorly within the embryo, away from the source and thus down the initial concentration gradient.
Notably, this is also true when de novo transcription is blocked, which rules out that expression of
putative factors propagates as a wave to shape the gradient and rather suggests that its activation
would have to be part of the mechanism of gradient formation. The factors (e.g. a receptor or a co-
factor/co-receptor) could be expressed in a fixed but broad enough domain to encompass the whole
PZ, and some specific event would potentiate its activity, for instance the contact with the VM.
Interestingly, this is what happens for integrins. Once expressed in the PZ before induction of wave
propagation, integrin transcription is no longer required and integrin activity is potentiated/activated
by the contact to the VM which itself propagates as a wave.”
• Interplay with integrins. Although integrins are involved in the Myosin-II pattern it is unclear if this
is an independent parallel regulation or it is involved in a functional interplay as illustrated in the
scheme in Fig. 6O. For instance, is integrin attachment also affecting the Smog/Fog gradient? Or is
it possible that Fog manipulations could affect the integrin complexes that impact the myosin
gradient? I suggest that the authors perform live imaging or immunostainings of i) integrin localization in
the diffusible vs tethered Fog or gprk2 embryos, and ii) Fog/smog gradient in the integrin manipulations. This
characterization would support the self-renew hypothesis.
Response: Our data in Fig. 6A-D show that integrins are required for the enhanced Fog-GPCR
signalling in gprk2 RNAi and suggest that integrins may regulate directly receptor activation and/or
its downstream signalling to MyoII. Notably, if integrins and GPCR signalling were parallel pathways
to regulate MyoII, we would observe that the effects of loss of integrins (i.e. decreased amplitude
with similar range of the gradient) and loss of Gprk2 (i.e. increased amplitude and range of the
gradient) would add to one another in the double LOF condition (gprk2 RNAi + αPS3-/-) and produce
an intermediate phenotype. The expected phenotype would then be an increased range of the MyoII
gradient compared to WT with an amplitude in between that of αPS3-/- and gprk2 RNAi embryos.
Instead, we observe that the phenotype of gprk2 RNAi + αPS3-/- is like that of αPS3-/- embryos,
8
indicating a functional interaction between GPCR signalling and integrins. We agree that this
functional interaction is an important point that deserves further investigation.
Impact of Fog on Integrin:
Concerning the modulation of integrin complexes by Fog-GPCR signalling, we show in Fig. 6H-N
that in gprk2 RNAi embryos both the amplitude and the range of gradient of integrin focal complexes
are increased in the PZ. These effects depend both on an increased activity of the positive feedback
of MyoII on integrins (Collinet et al., 2024, PMID: 38103554), which sustains the formation of focal
complexes, and on a larger zone of contact of the tissue with the vitelline membrane in gprk2 RNAi
embryos (Fig. S7G-I and Fig. S7J-K, now S8G-I and S8J-K). The latter may result from an increased
stiffness of the tissue due to increased MyoII levels; this would increase the range of tissue outward
bending next to regions of invagination and thus the range of contact with vitelline membrane.
Impact of Integrin on Fog signalling: To explain the functional interaction reported in Fig. 6A-D
we hypothesized that integrins might either directly promote receptor clustering or act as a co-factor
necessary for GPCR signalling amplification in the PZ. We thus measured the oligomerization of the
Fog receptor Smog in the PZ in αPS3 depleted (RNAi) embryos by FCS. We found that αPS3 RNAi
did not decrease Smog oligomerization in the PZ compared to WT embryos, as we expected if
integrins had a direct role of in receptor clustering. On the contrary, we observed an increase of Smog
oligomerization in αPS3 RNAi despite reduced signalling, as shown by the decreased MyoII levels
in both αPS3-/- and αPS3-/- + gprk2 RNAi embryos, Fig. 6A-D. This may reflect either a different
topology of the apical membrane (e.g. more apical membrane grooves in the WT which may
artificially decrease Smog molecular brightness) or a longer residence of inactive Smog oligomers at
the plasma membrane (the lack of receptor activation would also lead to its reduced endocytosis).
Together, based on these data we conclude that integrins do not regulate the Fog activity gradient by
promoting receptor clustering, but may do so by acting as a co-factor for GPCR signalling
amplification. We now present these data in a new panel in Fig. S8F.
These data support the view that the Fog-GPCR activity gradient emerges from tissue bending,
contact with the vitelline membrane, integrin activation, MyoII activation and tissue detachment in a
self-organised cycle.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Mundhe and colleagues identify an extracellular gradient of a GPCR ligand, Fog, and
explore how it can directly contribute to the formation of intracellular gradients of Myo2, a
contractile protein essential for successful Drosophila gastrulation. Their findings are interesting and
novel, and the authors go at length to characterize and quantify the dynamics of this system, specially
how the observed gradients can rapidly shape and influence the endoderm invagination
morphogenesis.
Both conceptually and methodologically, the work is relevant to the field. While the idea of
‘mechanogen’ is not new, the identification of mechanochemical coupling via the establishment of
chemical gradients that lead to direct activation of mechanically active downstream targets
(independently of transcription) is an important finding.
As is, the current study and respective analyses support part of the authors' claims. Further crucial
evidence and clarifications are required as detailed below to strengthen and validate the proposed
conclusions.
Major points:

While the overlap in anti-Fog signals generated from the KI line and wt conditions is rather nice
(Fig. 4E), as it would indicate that Fog regardless of being tagged is being produced and secreted to

anti-GFP is brighter? Can Fog::YFP rescue a fog-/- mutant?

polyclonal anti-GFP antibody raised in chickens and a polyclonal anti-Fog antibody raised in rabbits,

antibody was pre-adsorbed on embryos that do not express Fog to reduce non-specific binding and
labelling. This likely also reduces total signal. Finally, the two primary antibodies are revealed with
different secondary antibodies, labelled with different fluorophores (a donkey anti-chicken Alexa

## Paper

## Abstract

During development cell deformations are spatially organized, however, how cellular mechanics is spatially controlled is unclear. Spatial control of cell identity often determines local cellular mechanics in a two-tiered mechanism. Theoretical studies also proposed that molecular gradients, so called “mechanogens”, spatially control mechanics. We report evidence of a similar mechanism required for Drosophila gastrulation. We show that the GPCR ligand Fog, expressed in the posterior endoderm, diffuses and acts in a concentration-dependent manner to activate actomyosin contractility at a distance during a wave of tissue invagination. While Fog is uniformly distributed in the extracellular space, it forms a surface-bound gradient that recruits Myosin-II via receptor oligomerization. This activity gradient self-renews as the wave propagates and is shaped by both receptor endocytosis and modulation of GPCR signalling by integrins upon adhesion to the vitelline membrane. This exemplifies how chemical, mechanical and geometrical cues underly the emergence of a self-organized mechanogen activity gradient.

---

## Introduction

Embryonic development entails the spatial and temporal control of both cell fate determination to generate different cell types and of cell mechanics to generate tissue shapes during morphogenesis. Classically, the latter is considered to be a consequence of the former. For instance, the vertebrate nervous system is first specified in the dorsal region of the ectoderm and subsequently shaped into the neural tube. Similarly, the Drosophila mesoderm is first specified in the ventral part of the embryos, and then invaginates.

Typically, spatial patterning in a field of cells involves morphogens, i.e., diffusing molecules that form concentration gradients and impart positional information within tissues. Morphogens are produced from a source, from where they diffuse, and are degraded within the target tissue, thereby producing exponential gradients. Receiving cells interpret the positional information imparted by morphogen gradients by activating the expression of different genes at different morphogen concentration thresholds. This mechanism partitions the field of receiving cells into discrete domains with different cell identities. For example, the morphogens Shh, BMP and Wnt specify the identity of different neuron progenitors in the vertebrate neural tube through the expression of different combinations of transcription factors. In Drosophila, the morphogen Dorsal specifies mesoderm identity on the ventral side of embryos via the expression of the transcription factors Twist and Snail. Within this framework, the specification of cell identities directs downstream morphogenetic processes through the expression of molecular effectors that regulate cell mechanics, such as cell contractility, cell motility and cell adhesion. For example, the differential expression of adhesion molecules downstream of the Shh morphogen controls sorting of neural progenitors in the zebrafish neural tube. In the Drosophila ventral mesoderm, the transcription factors Twist and Snail, in response to the morphogen Dorsal, induce the expression of Fog, a GPCR ligand that leads to the apical activation of the small GTPase Rho1, the kinase Rok and non-muscle Myosin-II (MyoII). This induces cell-autonomous apical constriction and culminates with the invagination of the mesoderm in the ventral part of the embryos. Thus, morphogens direct morphogenesis via a two-tiered mechanism whereby the spatial control of cell identities determines downstream local cellular mechanics.

By analogy to the concept of morphogens, theoretical studies proposed that so-called “mechanogens”, i.e., “external diffusible bio-molecules”, may form spatial gradients that “influence mechanical properties, such as cell-cell adhesion and cellular contractility (and therefore, cell shape), and create spatial gradients in cell structure in a tissue”. Recent studies reported that classical morphogens can also function as mechanogens by regulating collective tissue mechanical properties without specifying cell fates. For instance, a gradient of Nodal in Zebrafish specifies mesendoderm invagination by two mechanisms: (1) triggering a motility-driven unjamming transition in protrusive leader cells able to autonomously internalize, and (2) promoting adhesion to their immediate followers, which results in a collective and ordered mode of internalization. Similarly, in the developing feather buds, the morphogens BMP and FGF define two adjacent domains with different supracellular mechanical properties, a rigid elastic core and an active fluid-like margin, that drive mesenchymal budding. In both cases, the morphogens Nodal and BMP can be considered to act as mechanogens as they tune collective, supracellular mechanical properties; however, they most likely do it indirectly via transcriptional regulation of target genes. Instead, mechanogens have been proposed to form chemical gradients that directly regulate cell mechanics (e.g., cell contractility) without the intermediary of gene transcription.

Here, we demonstrate that the GPCR ligand Fog, a signaling molecule directly controlling cellular contractility, in addition to its autocrine function in the Drosophila posterior midgut anlage, it diffuses away from its zone of production and acts in a concentration-dependent manner to control a gradient of MyoII activation during the propagation of a wave of tissue invagination. We show that, although Fog is homogenously distributed in the extracellular perivitelline fluid, it forms a multicellular scale activity gradient on the cell surface that constantly renews and propagates towards the anterior as the wave propagates. We propose that the Fog activity gradient patterns contractility in a manner similar to a mechanogen.

---

## Results

GPCR signaling is required in the propagation zone for MyoII activation
The morphogenesis of the Drosophila posterior endoderm begins with MyoII-dependent apical constriction in the posterior-most region of the embryo, the endoderm primordium. Here, the terminal transcription factors Hückebein and Tailless control the localized expression and secretion of the ligand Fog, which activates tissue autonomous recruitment of MyoII apically and tissue bending. This induces a polarized flow towards the embryo dorsal-anterior due to the high curvature of the tissue in this region. This initial flow and tissue bending triggers a wave of MyoII activation and tissue invagination that propagates anteriorly within the dorsal epithelium across a region denominated “wave propagation zone (PZ)”. Wave propagation does not depend on sustained gene transcription and is driven by a self-replicating cycle of 3D cell deformation where cells anterior to the furrow undergo a sequence: (1) contact with the vitelline membrane (VM), (2) integrin-mediated adhesion, (3) MyoII activation, and (4) detachment from the VM due to contractility in the furrow, as they get closer to the invaginating front. During the wave, MyoII is initially recruited at low levels in cells distant from the furrow upon their contact with the vitelline membrane. Then, when cells get closer to the furrow, MyoII recruitment rapidly increases via positive feedback, where integrins promote MyoII recruitment, which in turn stabilizes focal complexes in contact with the VM. Previous studies ruled out that the propagation of MyoII activation solely reflects the movement of the diffusion front of an expanding gradient of the ligand Fog away from the endoderm primordium. However, the requirement for Fog-GPCR signaling in the activation of MyoII in cells of the PZ was not directly tested. Furthermore, since in the absence of integrins (KO of the integrin α-PS3, also known as Scab), MyoII activation, which remains pulsatile at low levels, is not completely abolished during wave propagation, other factors, such as Fog-GPCR signaling, could be involved.

The small GTPase Gα Concertina (hereafter Gα) is known to transduce Fog-GPCR signaling that activates medio-apical MyoII contractility and tissue invagination in the endoderm and mesoderm primordia. In the absence of Gα (null mutants Gα−/−), invagination of the endoderm primordium, which triggers the subsequent wave propagation, is blocked. Thus, to test the role of Fog-GPCR signaling in cells of the PZ, we rescued Gα activity in Gα−/− embryos only in the primordium to be able to induce its invagination. To this end, we expressed a WT form of Gα using a hückebein (hkb) promoter, which drives expression specifically in the posterior endoderm primordium and not in the neighboring PZ, in Gα−/− embryos (Gα−/− hkb-Gα hereafter). We visualized cell contours with E-cadherin::GFP and MyoII recruitment with MyoII Regulatory Light Chain MRLC::mCherry. As expected, in Gα−/− hkb-Gα embryos, cells in the primordium recruited apical MyoII and constricted apically. This led to the formation of an initial invagination with kinetics similar to those in WT embryos, indicating a functional rescue of Gα activity in the primordium. However, despite a normal invagination of the endoderm primordium, in Gα−/− hkb-Gα embryos, the subsequent wave propagation and the dorsal-anterior movement of the posterior endoderm were severely affected. Indeed, MyoII propagation occurred on average only in 2.5 ± 0.06 (mean ± s.e.m.) rows of cells compared to an average of 7.1 ± 0.3 (mean ± s.e.m.) cells in WT embryos. Beyond the first two cells at the border with the endoderm primordium, in the PZ of Gα−/− hkb-Gα, MyoII was not recruited at all. As a result, non-contractile cells joined the furrow, which blocked detachment from the VM of more anterior cells once they reached the edge of the invaginating furrow.
Together, we conclude that Gα signaling in cells of the PZ is required to activate MyoII and sustain wave propagation.

Fog diffusion from the primordium is necessary for MyoII activation in the propagation zone
In Drosophila, Gα signaling inducing MyoII-dependent tissue invagination is activated by the secreted GPCR ligand Fog. We thus considered that Fog might be the ligand activating Gα signaling in the PZ. Consistent with this possibility, Fog protein was detected by immunohistochemistry in the PZ. In the posterior endoderm, fog is expressed zygotically at high levels only in the primordium region, but maternally deposited fog transcripts have been detected at low levels everywhere in the embryo and could give rise to Fog detected in the PZ. To test the roles of these two possible sources of Fog, we generated embryos where fog is expressed only zygotically in the endoderm primordium. To this end, we blocked both maternal and zygotic endogenous expression by injection of dsRNAs against fog (fog RNAi) and restored fog expression only in the endoderm primordium using an RNAi-resistant fog transgene expressed under the hkb promoter (hereafter hkb-fog res) (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Contrary to the expression of an RNAi-sensitive hkb-fog transgene (hkb-fog sen hereafter), expression of hkb-fog res in fog RNAi embryos rescued the invagination and the dorsal-anterior movement of the posterior endoderm, indicating that fog is indeed resistant to RNAi. Notably, hkb-fog res rescued apical MyoII recruitment, cell apical constriction and tissue invagination in the endoderm primordium, which were defective in hkb-fog sen embryos. Furthermore, hkb-fog res also rescued the propagation of MyoII in fog RNAi embryos. Propagation of MyoII in these embryos spanned on average 5.3 ± 0.2 (mean ± s.e.m.) cells while it was completely blocked in hkb-fog sen embryos injected with fog dsRNAs. Moreover, in hkb-fog res embryos injected with fog dsRNAs the levels of MyoII were almost as high as in hkb-fog res embryos injected with water, showing that fog expression in the endoderm primordium is sufficient to rescue endoderm invagination and wave propagation in fog RNAi embryos. We conclude that Fog produced in the endoderm primordium acts non-autonomously in the PZ to activate GPCR-dependent MyoII activation there.
Next, we investigated the mechanism by which Fog acts at a distance in the PZ. Fog is a large (100 kDa), secreted molecule and previous reports did not convincingly determine whether Fog acts in a paracrine manner. In light of the non-autonomous rescue of MyoII recruitment in the PZ reported above, we hypothesized that Fog produced and secreted in the primordium might diffuse into the PZ to activate MyoII. To test this, we sought to inhibit Fog dispersal from its source of production. We constructed a membrane-tethered version of Fog by fusing the entire fog coding sequence with a truncated form (Δ1–421, see methods for details) of the vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) G protein, a type-II transmembrane protein, and tested its ability to disperse from a localized production source. We expressed Fog-VSV-GΔ1–421 (Fog VSV-G hereafter) in stripes in the embryo using the wingless-Gal4 driver and visualized it with an anti-Fog antibody. Contrary to a WT version of Fog that was detected also into the neighboring non-expressing tissue, Fog VSV-G was only observed within the producing cells. To test the ability of Fog VSV-G to activate MyoII, we overexpressed it homogeneously in the embryo during gastrulation. The resulting MyoII pattern with low-level recruitment in the entire dorsal epithelium and strong MyoII apical recruitment in the endoderm primordium and the PZ, was similar to that of an overexpressed WT Fog. This confirmed that Fog VSV-G, although unable to diffuse, is able to activate GPCR signaling and MyoII contractility cell-autonomously in the embryo. We next used this tool to test whether Fog produced in the primordium diffuses to the PZ to activate MyoII there. We expressed an RNAi-resistant version of Fog VSV-G, in the primordium (using the hkb promoter) in embryos injected with fog dsRNA to remove endogenous maternal and zygotic Fog (hereafter referred to as hkb-fog VSV-G, Fig. 2b). In hkb-fog VSV-G embryos, cell apical constriction and endoderm primordium invagination were similar to hkb-fog res. However, the subsequent anterior movement of the endoderm was blocked as was wave propagation (on average only 1.7 ± 0.1 (mean ± s.e.m.) cells). Indeed, in hkb-fog VSV-G embryos, MyoII was not recruited apically in cells of the PZ beyond the first 1–2 cell rows, and cells did not detach from the VM.
Altogether, we conclude that Fog produced in the primordium diffuses into the zone of wave propagation, where it is required to activate apical MyoII contractility and cell detachment. Our findings demonstrate that Fog acts in a tissue non-autonomous manner during wave propagation.

Fog production and uptake tune an exponential gradient of MyoII
Since Fog diffuses from the primordium to activate MyoII at a distance, we next explored the spatial dynamics of Fog activity. During wave propagation, apical MyoII is graded in a restricted domain of 2–3 cell rows over ~30–40 μm from the advancing furrow, with high MyoII levels in cells just anterior to the furrow and lower levels more anteriorly. We considered the possibility that Fog diffusion from the primordium and degradation or removal in the receptive field may set the amplitude and range of this graded pattern of MyoII in a manner similar to morphogen activity gradients. We found that at each moment in time, as the invaginating furrow moves toward the anterior, the spatial distribution of apical MyoII mean intensity in front of the furrow fits a one-phase exponential decay curve with an average length-scale (λ) of 3.18 ± 0.29 (mean ± s.e.m.) μm. The shape of the activity gradient of morphogens typically depends on (1) the rate of morphogen production at the source, (2) the rate of its removal in the target tissue, and (3) its diffusion coefficient. We tested whether similar mechanisms also control the gradient of MyoII in the PZ. To this end, we first increased Fog production in the primordium (the source) by expressing two additional copies of a WT form of Fog using the hkb promoter. This increased both the amplitude in front of the invaginating furrow (at x=0 μm, WT: 11.55 ± 0.10 A.U and hkb-fog: 32.59 ± 0.32 A.U (mean ± s.e.m.)) and the range of the gradient (WT: 27.08 ± 5.72 μm, hkb-fog: greater than 38.01 ± 1.92 μm (mean ± s.e.m.), see methods) as expected of a concentration gradient that defines the activation profile of MyoII. Interestingly, the length scale of the exponential MyoII gradient also increased (WT: 3.18 ± 0.29 μm and hkb-fog: 5.26 ± 0.58 μm, (mean ± s.e.m.)), suggesting that diffusion or degradation/removal of Fog may depend on Fog concentration. Next, we tested whether the spatial gradient of MyoII also depends on Fog removal within the PZ. Since Fog binding to its GPCR induces endocytosis of the receptor-ligand complex, we sought to interfere with Fog removal by blocking GPCR endocytosis. Gprk2, a kinase that promotes GPCR endocytosis upon ligand binding, is the only GRK known to interfere with Fog signaling and endocytosis in the embryo. Knock-down of Gprk2 by RNAi (gprk2 RNAi) resulted in an increase in the amplitude (Control: 9.72 ± 0.08 A.U and gprk2 RNAi: 14.25 ± 0.14 A.U (mean ± s.e.m.)), the range (Control: 20.86 ± 5.72 μm and gprk2 RNAi: greater than 33.59 ± 2.5 μm (mean ± s.e.m.)) and length-scale (Control: 2.96 ± 0.45 μm and gprk2 RNAi: 5.48 ± 0.58 μm (mean ± s.e.m.)) of the exponential MyoII profile similar to hkb-fog, indicating that Fog removal/endocytosis also tunes the MyoII gradient.
Thus, Fog produced in the endoderm primordium sets an exponential gradient of MyoII in the PZ by diffusion/degradation. Furthermore, since we find that the shape of this gradient is not perturbed when gene transcription was blocked with α-amanitin, Fog acts non transcriptionally in the PZ. These findings suggest that Fog might act as a mechanogen directly controlling cellular contractility. It is worth noting that this exponential gradient, whose maximum is located at the edge of the tissue invagination, is not static but translocates anteriorly as the wave of invagination propagates to the anterior.

Fog is uniformly distributed in the extracellular space
Since Fog regulates the gradient of MyoII in the PZ, we next tested whether Fog also forms a concentration gradient there. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) against Fog in fixed embryos revealed a concentration gradient of cellular Fog protein in the PZ, although shallower than that of MyoII, consistent with the integrin-dependent amplification of MyoII activation closer to the invaginating furrow. This concentration gradient may reflect intracellular or surface-bound Fog since the soluble extracellular fraction is washed away during fixation and permeabilization. To visualize the entire pool of Fog protein in living embryos (extracellular and intracellular), we engineered an endogenous Fog::SYFP2 protein fusion at the fog locus using CRISPR/Cas9 (referred to as Fog::YFP). Fog::YFP homozygote flies were viable and their embryos showed no defects in gastrulation. Furthermore, IHC to detect Fog::YFP with antibodies anti-GFP (to visualize the YFP tag) and anti-Fog (to visualize the Fog portion of the fusion protein) showed (1) a localization consistent with that of the known endogenous protein in both the endoderm primordium (subapical vesicular accumulation) and the PZ (shallow apical gradient) and (2) a high degree of co-localization between the two detection methods. Altogether these results indicate that Fog::YFP is functional and correctly localized. In particular, they also suggest that Fog::YFP is not cleaved in the embryo despite the presence of three putative protein cleavage sites in the Fog protein sequence. To further test this latter possibility, we measured the diffusion coefficient (D) of Fog::YFP in the extracellular space using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS). Within the extracellular space between the VM and the invaginated posterior endoderm, Fog::YFP exhibited significantly slower diffusion dynamics than secreted GFP at comparable excitation power. To circumvent artifacts induced by photophysical effects, we interpolated the values of D obtained from FCS measurements at different excitation powers. We thereby obtained for Fog::YFP a D of 55 μm2 s−1, as predicted for a globular 127 kDa protein diffusing in an aqueous fluid and for a secreted version of GFP a significantly higher D = 87 μm2 s−1 (sec::GFP, 27 kDa). Thus, Fog::YFP is a good Fog reporter in vivo and we used it to image Fog distribution during wave propagation.
In contrast to our expectations and the fact that intracellular Fog forms a gradient, we observed that Fog::YFP was present in the extracellular perivitelline space at uniform concentration. The distribution of Fog::YFP across the region of wave propagation was similar to that of sec::GFP, which reflects the available space between the apical surface of cells and the VM. Thus, endogenous Fog::YFP is uniformly distributed in the extracellular perivitelline space during wave propagation. This does not depend on the presence of a maternal protein pool since a similar distribution was observed also when Fog::YFP was expressed only zygotically with a hkb promoter.
We conclude that extracellular Fog does not exhibit a concentration gradient in the PZ. Yet, intracellular Fog and its signaling (MyoII activation) are restricted to a dynamic domain of few cells anterior to the advancing furrow. This argues that Fog dependent signaling is organized at the cell surface in a dynamic spatial gradient, as the tissue invagination wave propagates anteriorly.

GPCR endocytosis tunes a gradient of cell-surface bound Fog and receptor oligomerization
This led us to investigate how a gradient of MyoII activation emerges in the PZ in spite of uniform extracellular Fog in the vitelline fluid. To test this, we analyzed the diffusion dynamics of Fog at the apical surface of cells in the PZ using FCS. In contrast to our measurements in the extracellular space within the posterior invagination, in the PZ we observed two populations of Fog, characterized by two distinct diffusion coefficients. A large fraction of Fog (84% of the total pool) displayed an average diffusion coefficient D of 51 ± 2 (mean ± s.e.m.) μm2 s−1 (D fast), similar to that measured in the posterior invagination and indicative of free diffusion. A minor fraction of Fog (16% of the total pool) showed much slower diffusion dynamics, with an average D of 1.6 ± 0.2 (mean ± s.e.m.) μm2 s−1 (D slow). This presumably corresponds to ligands bound to or interacting with the apical plasma membrane of cells, since it was undetectable in measurements within the extracellular space performed inside the invagination. Interestingly, the average diffusion coefficient of the Fog receptor Smog::GFP (0.54 ± 0.04 (mean ± s.e.m.) μm2 s−1) at the apical cell surface in the PZ measured by FCS was in the same range, but nonetheless significantly lower than D slow of Fog. This suggests that the slow-diffusing fraction of Fog (Fog slow) could correspond to ligands transiently bound to their receptor in the PZ. To further test this, we sought to increase the half-life of the receptor at the surface by inhibiting GPCR endocytosis (gprk2 RNAi) and measured Fog slow in the PZ. We found that in gprk2 RNAi embryos the Fog slow fraction increased to 30 ± 15% (mean ± s.e.m.) of the total pool from 16 ± 1% (mean ± s.e.m.) in WT, consistent with the idea that Fog slow is receptor-bound on the surface of cells in the PZ. We next examined whether Fog slow forms a spatial gradient in the PZ. We found that in WT embryos Fog slow was higher closer to the invagination (0–20 μm) than further away (20–70 μm) and that a spatial gradient with a negative slope could be detected within each embryo. Furthermore, blocking GPCR endocytosis not only globally increased Fog slow but also significantly reduced the average slope of its gradient, which was now not different from 0. These results are consistent with the observed higher levels of MyoII and its expanded gradient in gprk2 RNAi embryos and suggest that the Fog activity gradient might emerge from a gradient of ligand-receptor binding within the PZ.
Next, we sought to measure Fog receptor activation within the PZ to see if that also formed a gradient as predicted from the distribution of Fog slow. GPCR ligand binding and activation is known to induce receptor clustering (oligomerization), which can be measured by FCS. Using FCS, we measured the per-particle brightness, which reflects the degree of molecular oligomerization, of Smog::GFP on the cell apical surface in the PZ. Consistent with previous studies, we found that the molecular brightness of Smog::GFP decreased upon depletion of the ligand Fog and increased upon depletion of Gprk2 without changing its diffusion coefficient and only slightly affecting its total concentration. We next compared molecular brightness of Smog::GFP with that of the known trimeric protein VSV-G::GFP and found that the brightness of VSV-G::GFP was significantly higher than that of Smog::GFP in both the PZ and the lateral ectoderm. Furthermore, since VSV-G::GFP brightness was not affected by neither Fog nor Gprk2 depletion, these results confirmed that the observed effects on Smog::GFP are receptor specific and that its oligomerization is a proxy for GPCR activation. The comparison of molecular brightness with VSV-G::GFP also suggests that, in the simplest scenario, Smog::GFP is present as a mixture of dimers and monomers in WT embryos, while oligomerization increases upon blocking receptor endocytosis and decreases in the absence of the ligand Fog during wave propagation. Since our data indicate that Smog::GFP exists as monomers and higher-order oligomers (dimers, trimers, etc.), we next estimated the fraction of oligomers from the measured brightness, assuming a linear dependence of the brightness on the number of protomers. Since only the average brightness can be directly extracted from FCS measurements, the exact type of oligomeric species cannot be determined. Nevertheless, for a particular model, i.e., a two-species mixture of monomers and oligomers, the fraction of monomers and oligomers can be estimated. We calculated these numbers for several possible scenarios (monomers with either dimers, trimers or tetramers) in WT, fog and gprk2 RNAi embryos taking previously reported photophysical properties of GFP into account. Depleting the ligand Fog by RNAi reduced the probability of higher-order oligomer formation for Smog::GFP by ~8 folds, i.e., from ~68% dimers in WT embryos to less than 8% in fog RNAi embryos. Conversely, blocking receptor endocytosis significantly increased oligomer formation by ~21% when considering the coupled dimers/monomers (from 79 to 100%) or by ~55% when considering the coupled trimers/monomers (from 21 to 76%). To test whether Smog::GFP oligomers are distributed in a gradient in the PZ, we measured Smog::GFP brightness on the apical cell surface and at lateral junctions as a function of the distance from the invaginating furrow in the PZ. In WT embryos we found higher Smog::GFP brightness closer to the invagination (0–20 μm) than at larger distances (20–70 μm), and spatial gradients with negative slopes within each embryo on the apical surface and similar, although less significant, trends at junctions. gprk2 RNAi reduced this spatial difference by increasing Smog::GFP brightness both close and at a distance from the invagination and significantly changed the average slope of the gradients observed within each embryo, which were now not different from 0 or even slightly positive, indicating that the gradient of Smog::GFP oligomerization depends on GPCR endocytosis. Importantly, this spatial dependence of oligomerization was specific to Smog::GFP, as no gradient was observed for VSV-G::GFP. Altogether, our data indicate that Fog binding to the cell apical surface induces a gradient of receptor activation and oligomerization, which is tuned by receptor endocytosis.

Integrin activation by contact with the vitelline membrane tunes the Fog activity gradient
The gradient of GPCR activation and oligomerization tunes the multicellular spatial pattern of MyoII activation during wave propagation. Integrins, which are activated when cells of the PZ contact the VM, are also involved in MyoII activation. We showed earlier that the αPS3 integrin Scab amplifies MyoII levels in a positive feedback mechanism. Consistent with this, in αPS3 null mutants (αPS3−/−), MyoII was recruited at much lower levels than in WT embryos, although higher than those observed in the absence of Gα signaling. Moreover, in these mutants, MyoII recruitment in the PZ still followed an exponential gradient with a range similar to WT, albeit with lower amplitude, which led to an increased length scale compared to WT embryos. This suggests that amplification of MyoII activation by integrins is not uniform in the PZ, as the gradient length scale should not change with a uniform amplification by a constant factor. This led us to address whether integrins only amplify MyoII activation in the cell near the edge of invagination front, as previously suggested, or whether they also have a role in regulating the spatial range of the multicellular Fog/GPCR activity gradient. Since amplitude, range and length scale of the gradient are increased significantly when GPCR endocytosis is inhibited in gprk2 RNAi embryos, we tested whether integrins are required for this effect and thus for the process of gradient formation by acting everywhere in the field where Fog and GPCR signaling can be active. Strikingly, removing integrins in embryos depleted for Gprk2 (gprk2 RNAi + αPS3−/−) dramatically reduced both the levels and the range of MyoII to levels similar to those of the knock-out of integrins (αPS3−/−). These results show that integrins are required for both the expanded gradient and the higher levels of MyoII observed following the hyperactivation of Fog-GPCR signaling. Additionally, it shows that blocking endocytosis has no impact on the shape of the gradient if integrins are absent. We conclude that integrins are part of the multicellular gradient formation mechanism and do not simply amplify MyoII activation in the cell near the invagination front. Next, we tested whether integrins directly promote oligomerization of GPCR and thus MyoII recruitment as part of the gradient formation mechanism. We measured the molecular brightness of Smog::GFP by FCS in the PZ of embryos depleted of the αPS3 integrin Scab by RNAi (αPS3 RNAi), and we found that this was not decreased compared to WT embryos, contrary to what would be expected if integrins promoted Smog oligomerization. Smog::GFP molecular brightness was instead increased in the PZ compared to WT, suggesting that in the absence of integrins, Smog::GFP oligomers are no longer active (decreased MyoII levels, despite higher molecular clustering). We conclude that integrins do not directly promote GPCR clustering as part of the gradient formation mechanism, but rather they act as co-factors for GPCR oligomer signaling.
Integrins accumulate and form bright puncta in the PZ upon apical cell contact with the overlying vitelline membrane. The range of this contact might thus contribute to determining the range of the gradient of MyoII and GPCR signaling. Consistent with this idea, integrin puncta, visualized with the endogenously GFP-tagged βPS integrin Myospheroid (βPS::GFP hereafter), accumulated at highest levels closer to the invaginating furrow and decreased more anteriorly forming a gradient with a range identical to that of MyoII activation in the PZ. This integrin gradient formed within the region of contact of the tissue with the VM, as revealed by the exclusion of dextran injected in the perivitelline space from the region where βPS::GFP forms bright puncta. Furthermore, the depletion of Gprk2 increased the amplitude and the range of the gradient of βPS::GFP as well as the range of tissue contact with the VM (monitored by the exclusion of dextran and by the distance of E-cad junctions from the VM), suggesting that the increased range of the MyoII gradient observed in these mutants stems from a larger zone of contact with the VM in front of the invaginating furrow.
Together, we conclude that during wave propagation, MyoII is activated where integrins are in contact with the VM and that the range of the exponential gradient of MyoII during wave propagation depends on the contact of the tissue with the VM in a manner that involves integrin activation and their cross-talk with Fog-GPCR signaling.
